title: How Much of the Web Does ChatGPT Actually Use?
metaTitle: How Much of the Web Does ChatGPT Use? Training vs Live
metaDescription: ChatGPT trains on a filtered slice of the web and cites about 15 pages per live answer in one 2026 audit. The documented numbers, and what you can still change.
primaryKeyword: how much of the web does chatgpt use
shortAnswer: A small, filtered slice, and a different slice for each job. For training, OpenAI's last full disclosure (GPT-3) kept 570GB of Common Crawl text out of 45TB; for GPT-6 Astra it gives only a bracket of more than 10 trillion tokens. For a live answer, ChatGPT with search cited about 15 sources per response in one 2026 audit. The training slice is closed. The live slice is where you can still change the outcome.
intro:
"Does ChatGPT use the whole internet?" is the wrong question, because nobody publishes a count of the whole web to divide by. The useful question is which slice of the web ChatGPT draws on for each job, and whether your pages are inside it.

Below are the figures OpenAI and Common Crawl have actually published, the one 2026 audit that counts citations, and what our own crawler study shows about who keeps themselves out. Where a number does not exist, we say so.

sections.heading: How much of the web was ChatGPT trained on?
sections.body:
OpenAI published exact figures only for GPT-3. Its [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165) says the Common Crawl portion was 45TB of compressed plain text before filtering and 570GB after, roughly 400 billion tokens. For GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI's [public training summary](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/gpt-6-astra-eu-ai-act-public-summary-of-training-content.pdf) gives only a bracket: text of "more than 10 trillion tokens", the top option on the EU template.

The 570GB figure is the Common Crawl part alone, not the whole GPT-3 corpus. The paper's mix looks like this:

- **Common Crawl, filtered:** 410 billion tokens, 60% of the training mix, seen 0.44 times.
- **WebText2:** 19 billion tokens, 22% of the mix, seen 2.9 times.
- **Books1 and Books2:** 12 and 55 billion tokens, 8% each.
- **Wikipedia:** 3 billion tokens, 3% of the mix, seen 3.4 times.

Those weights were chosen, not proportional to size: higher-quality sources were sampled more often. Wikipedia, the smallest dataset, was read 3.4 times while the crawl was read less than once.

The tables total about 499 billion tokens, so Astra's bracket is more than 20 times larger on paper. Treat that as a rough comparison, because the two documents define "size" differently.

Astra's summary also confirms the training mix is not only the open web. It lists Common Crawl, data accessed through partnerships, synthetic data generated with earlier OpenAI models and, subject to privacy settings, interactions from products such as ChatGPT. For GPTBot crawling it gives a collection period of approximately March 2013 to May 2026, and says the crawler is designed to respect robots.txt.

![Rows of library shelves holding books in soft light, with a focused view on the spines](https://images.pexels.com/photos/990432/pexels-photo-990432.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&w=1200)

sections.heading: How big is Common Crawl, and is it the whole web?
sections.body:
Common Crawl describes its own dataset as a sample. Its [FAQ](https://commoncrawl.org/faq) says it does not generally archive entire websites, only "a randomly selected subset" of each. Its [September 2026 crawl](https://commoncrawl.org/blog/september-2026-crawl-archive-now-available) holds 2.17 billion pages, 361.4 TiB uncompressed, from 40.4 million hosts and 33.2 million registered domains.

That is one monthly snapshot of a rotating sample, not a cumulative copy of the web.

We found no authoritative count of the whole web, so we do not quote a "percent of the web". Any page that does is guessing. What is documented: Common Crawl is a rotating sample, OpenAI filters it, and the filtered result is one input among several.

CCBot, Common Crawl's crawler, checks robots.txt before fetching a page, per the same FAQ. The FAQ does not say a block removes crawls already collected; it points to a separate opt-out registry for that.

sections.heading: How much does ChatGPT read for a live answer?
sections.body:
OpenAI publishes no fixed number, and it varies by search depth. In a [2026 audit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23684) of 712 politics, health and environment questions put to four AI search engines, ChatGPT with web search cited 14.7 sources per response on average. That was the highest of the four, ahead of Copilot (8.4), Perplexity (7.9) and Gemini (7.3).

The count moves with the topic. ChatGPT cited roughly 20 sources per response on environment questions, 12 on health and 10 on politics. Citations are also a floor on pages read, not a ceiling.

Search depth changes the picture. OpenAI's [web search guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-web-search) says deep research "often" taps hundreds of sources and can run for several minutes, while plain non-reasoning search returns the top results with no planning step.

The audit found a long tail. The 25 most-cited domains made up 29.9% of ChatGPT's citations, and 82.8% of the domains it cited appeared twice or fewer times. A page does not need to be famous to be read. It needs to be one of the few that fit that particular question.

Limits: the audit covered three topics, drove each engine's web interface, and counts citations, not every page fetched.

![A woman works on a laptop inside a modern data center lined with mirrored server racks](https://images.pexels.com/photos/1181316/pexels-photo-1181316.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&w=1200)

sections.heading: How does ChatGPT choose which pages to read?
sections.body:
OpenAI documents the mechanics, not the ranking recipe. The model decides whether to search, sends queries to a search tool and, in agentic mode, reads results and decides whether to keep going. Which pages win beyond that is observed behavior, not published policy.

Be wary of anyone quoting exact ranking weights for ChatGPT. None are public. What you can verify is simpler:

- Your page has to be fetchable by OpenAI's search crawler: per its [crawler documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots), sites that opt out of OAI-SearchBot are not shown in ChatGPT search answers.
- Our advice, not a documented rule: lead each page with a direct answer, because retrieval matches pages to a specific question.
- Our stance: one strong page per question beats five thin ones, for Google and for AI retrieval.

For the selection logic in detail, read [how ChatGPT chooses its sources](/answers/how-does-chatgpt-choose-sources). For the retrieval mechanism underneath, see [what RAG is](/blog/what-is-rag).

sections.heading: Who blocks the crawlers that feed both slices?
sections.body:
Few brands do, and publishers often do. In AEOeye's crawler access study (October 2026, 384 sites), 44 sites (11.5%) blocked CCBot, 35 (9.1%) blocked GPTBot and 16 (4.2%) blocked OAI-SearchBot, which OpenAI's crawler documentation ties to ChatGPT search.

The split by group is the story:

| Blocks CCBot | Sites |
|---|---|
| News publishers | 29 of 38 (76.3%) |
| E-commerce and consumer brands | 5 of 90 (5.6%) |
| SaaS brands | 5 of 193 (2.6%) |
| AI-visibility vendors | 0 of 43 |

Our reading: the open crawl may lean away from publishers and toward brands, who mostly leave the door open. Being in the pool is not the same as being remembered, but a block guarantees you are not in it.

Limits: it is a convenience sample of established sites, fetched once on one day, main host only, and robots.txt is a request, not enforcement. See the [study hub](/blog/ai-crawler-user-agent-directory) and the [per-site CSV](/resources/ai-crawler-access-study-2026-10.csv).

sections.heading: What should you do about it?
sections.body:
Spend your effort on the slice you can still change. Keep crawlers allowed, make each key fact easy to fetch and quote, and check whether ChatGPT actually cites you. You cannot enter a model that has already finished training.

1. **Decide on training and search separately.** They are controlled by different crawlers. We allow GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, CCBot and Applebot-Extended on aeoeye.com, because our business is being found. Our case against blanket blocking is in [why blocking GPTBot is usually a mistake](/blog/blocking-gptbot-is-usually-a-mistake).
2. **Generate a clean robots.txt** with the [AI Robots.txt Generator](/tools/ai-robots-txt-generator), then confirm in your CDN or firewall logs that the bots are not challenged. In our study 60 of 375 homepages (16%) challenged our self-identifying crawler.
3. **Lead each page with a direct answer** to one question. Retrieval reads pages that match the question, not pages that match the topic.
4. **Test, do not assume.** Ask ChatGPT your buyers' questions and see who it names. AEOeye's [free audit](/) asks ChatGPT three unbranded buyer questions live and shows the full answers.

rows.label: What it is
values: Text, images and other data used to build the model's weights; frozen once training ends
Pages fetched at question time and cited in the answer

rows.label: Documented scale
values: GPT-3: 570GB filtered Common Crawl text; GPT-6 Astra: more than 10 trillion tokens of text (bracket)
About 15 cited sources per response in one 2026 audit; deep research often hundreds

rows.label: Freshness
values: As current as the pages fetched

rows.label: Can you influence it now?
values: Only through crawl permissions for future runs

keyTakeaways: OpenAI published exact training figures only for GPT-3: 45TB of Common Crawl text filtered to 570GB. For GPT-6 Astra it gives a bracket of more than 10 trillion tokens.
Common Crawl calls its data a sample of the web; its September 2026 crawl held 2.17 billion pages from 33.2 million registered domains.
One 2026 audit counted 14.7 cited sources per ChatGPT search response, varying by topic, with a long tail: 82.8% of cited domains appeared twice or fewer times.
In AEOeye's crawler study, 76.3% of news publishers blocked CCBot against 2.6% of SaaS sites; brands rarely lock themselves out.
You cannot enter finished training data, so keep crawlers allowed and make pages fetchable and answer-first.

faqs.q: How much data does ChatGPT use in total?
faqs.a: It depends on the job and the model. OpenAI's last detailed disclosure, for GPT-3, kept 570GB of filtered Common Crawl text. For GPT-6 Astra it gives only a bracket of more than 10 trillion tokens of text. For one live answer, an audit counted about 15 cited sources for ChatGPT with search.

faqs.q: Does ChatGPT use the entire internet?
faqs.a: No. Common Crawl calls its dataset a sample of the web, OpenAI filters what it takes, and live answers cite a few to a few dozen pages. No authoritative count of the whole web exists, so any exact percentage is a guess.

faqs.q: What percentage of ChatGPT's training came from Common Crawl?
faqs.a: For GPT-3, filtered Common Crawl carried 60% of the training mix, WebText2 22%, two book corpora 16% and Wikipedia 3%, per OpenAI's paper. For newer models OpenAI names Common Crawl as a source but publishes no percentages, so any figure for them is unsourced.

faqs.q: Can I stop ChatGPT from using my website?
faqs.a: You can ask. Disallowing GPTBot in robots.txt tells OpenAI not to use your pages for training, and Common Crawl's CCBot has its own rule. Blocking is a request that governs future crawling, not a takedown tool, and blocking OAI-SearchBot removes you from ChatGPT search answers.

faqs.q: How can I tell if ChatGPT uses my pages?
faqs.a: Ask ChatGPT the questions your buyers ask and look at which sources it cites. Check your server or CDN logs for GPTBot and OAI-SearchBot requests. A free AEOeye audit asks ChatGPT three buyer questions live and shows whether your brand comes up.

definitions.definition: A nonprofit that crawls the web and freely provides its archives to the public; its monthly crawls are a sample of the web, not a copy of it, and are widely used as raw text for training language models.
The unit of text a language model processes, roughly a word fragment. GPT-3's filtered Common Crawl portion was about 410 billion tokens.
A technique that lets a language model retrieve and incorporate new information from external sources before answering, which is how ChatGPT's live search adds pages beyond its training data.
